meta.title: Supabase vs Appwrite (2026): Which option should you choose?
meta.description: Supabase vs Appwrite in 2026: compare database, auth, storage, functions, self-hosting, and pricing models to pick the right backend for your team.

verdict: Choose Supabase if you want a Postgres-first platform with SQL, Row Level Security, realtime, and an ecosystem built around relational data. Choose Appwrite if you prefer a broader multi-service backend with abstractions over multiple databases, and you value a single Docker-based self-hosted stack. Both are mature open-source options in 2026, but fit depends on your data model, hosting preferences, and team skills.

comparison.category: Core database model and query flexibility
comparison.toolA: Supabase is built around PostgreSQL, so you get full SQL, joins, views, extensions, and transactions. Its client libraries and auto-generated APIs reflect relational tables, and complex analytical queries are first-class rather than bolted on. Advanced features depend on the Postgres version and extensions you enable.
comparison.toolB: Appwrite provides a document-style database abstraction with collections, attributes, and permissions, and it can also run on top of databases such as MariaDB or PostgreSQL depending on deployment. That simplifies CRUD for app-style data but gives less direct control over raw SQL and relational modeling. Complex reporting may require custom functions or a separate data store.

comparison.toolA: Supabase Auth includes email/password, magic links, OAuth providers, phone auth, and JWT-based sessions, and it integrates tightly with Row Level Security so database access can be tied directly to authenticated users. Features and provider lists can change by plan, so confirm availability for your target version.
comparison.toolB: Appwrite offers a mature accounts service with sessions, OAuth, email and phone verification, teams, and role-based permissions. Its permission model spans users, teams, and roles across databases, storage, and functions, which can reduce custom authorization code. The exact provider set and limits vary by release and plan.

comparison.toolA: Supabase Edge Functions run on Deno and are useful for webhooks, third-party API calls, and lightweight business logic close to your data. For heavier workloads, database functions in Postgres and external services may be better, so teams often combine approaches. Runtime limits and cold-start behavior depend on plan and configuration.
comparison.toolB: Appwrite Functions support multiple runtimes, including Node.js, Python, PHP, Ruby, and others depending on version, and can be triggered by events, schedules, or HTTP. This flexibility suits mixed-language teams, though resource limits and execution timeouts are plan- and configuration-dependent.

comparison.toolA: Supabase Storage provides buckets, access policies via RLS, signed URLs, and image transformations for common needs. It is well suited to projects already using Postgres permissions, while very large-scale media pipelines may need a dedicated CDN or object store. Limits and transformation features vary by plan.
comparison.toolB: Appwrite Storage includes buckets, file-level permissions, previews, and integrations with its broader permissions system. It is convenient for apps that already use Appwrite auth and teams, and it supports multiple storage adapters in self-hosted setups depending on configuration.

comparison.toolA: Supabase Realtime can broadcast database changes, presence, and messages, making it practical for collaborative and live-updating apps. It uses Postgres logical replication for change streams, so behavior depends on table setup and publication configuration. Scale characteristics depend on plan and workload.
comparison.toolB: Appwrite Realtime supports subscriptions to documents, files, and other resources with channel-based permissions. It is straightforward for app-style realtime updates, but very high-throughput scenarios should be validated against your deployment and version.

comparison.toolA: Supabase can be self-hosted via Docker, but its stack includes multiple services, so production self-hosting requires Kubernetes or comparable orchestration experience. The hosted offering reduces operational burden, while self-hosting gives control over data residency and customization. Feature parity between hosted and self-hosted can differ.
comparison.toolB: Appwrite is designed to be self-hosted with a comparatively compact Docker-based deployment, which many teams find easier to run on a single server or small cluster. It supports multiple databases and storage adapters in self-hosted mode, though very large deployments still need careful capacity planning.

comparison.toolA: Supabase offers official client libraries for JavaScript, Python, Flutter, Swift, Kotlin, and more, plus a SQL editor, migrations, and a growing extension ecosystem. Developers comfortable with SQL tend to feel at home quickly, while those avoiding SQL face a steeper start.
comparison.toolB: Appwrite provides SDKs across web, mobile, and server platforms with consistent service-oriented APIs, and its console emphasizes guided setup. The abstraction layer can speed up standard app features, though it may feel restrictive for teams wanting direct database control.

comparison.toolA: Supabase uses tiered plans with usage-based add-ons for database size, bandwidth, storage, and compute, and self-hosting is available at infrastructure cost. Actual spend depends on workload and plan, so model your expected usage rather than assuming a fixed price.
comparison.toolB: Appwrite Cloud uses tiered plans with usage limits, and self-hosting is free for the software while you pay for infrastructure. Cost predictability depends on your traffic, function executions, and storage, so review current plan details for your version.

faq.q: Which is better for a relational app with complex SQL reporting?
faq.a: Supabase is usually the stronger fit because PostgreSQL is the primary database, giving you joins, views, transactions, and extensions without workarounds. Appwrite's document-style abstraction is convenient for app CRUD but less suited to heavy relational reporting. If analytics are central to your product, choose Supabase or pair Appwrite with a separate analytical store.

faq.q: Is Appwrite easier to self-host than Supabase?
faq.a: Appwrite is generally simpler to self-host because it ships as a comparatively compact Docker-based stack with a guided installer. Supabase self-hosting involves more services and is better suited to teams with container orchestration experience. Always validate the current self-hosting documentation for your target version.

faq.q: Can both tools handle authentication and permissions securely?
faq.a: Both provide mature authentication and authorization features, but the models differ: Supabase ties access to PostgreSQL Row Level Security, while Appwrite uses users, teams, roles, and resource-level permissions. Security depends heavily on correct policy configuration in either tool. Review the current security documentation and plan before production.

faq.q: Which platform is better for mobile and Flutter apps?
faq.a: Both offer mobile SDKs, including Flutter support, so the decision often comes down to data model and team skills. Supabase suits apps needing relational queries and realtime Postgres changes, while Appwrite's service abstractions can speed up standard auth, storage, and database features. Test the current SDKs against your app's requirements.

faq.q: Do I need SQL knowledge to use Supabase?
faq.a: Basic SQL knowledge helps significantly with Supabase, especially for policies, migrations, and complex queries. Simple CRUD can be done through client libraries, but advanced use of Row Level Security and reporting benefits from SQL fluency. Teams without SQL experience should budget learning time or consider Appwrite.

faq.q: Which tool is more cost-effective for a small startup?
faq.a: Both offer hosted tiers and free self-hosting options, and costs depend on your usage of database, storage, bandwidth, and functions. Comparing current plan details against realistic projections matters more than headline pricing. Self-hosting can lower software cost but adds operational overhead.

faq.q: Can Supabase and Appwrite replace a custom backend entirely?
faq.a: They cover common backend needs such as auth, database, storage, functions, and realtime, which can replace much custom backend code. Neither removes the need for domain logic, integrations, and security review, and some workloads may still require dedicated services. Treat them as accelerators rather than a complete substitute for architecture decisions.

faq.q: Which should I choose if I want multi-language serverless functions?
faq.a: Appwrite generally offers broader runtime support for functions, including several languages depending on version, which suits mixed-language teams. Supabase Edge Functions are Deno-based, with additional logic often placed in PostgreSQL functions. Confirm current runtime support and limits for your deployment.
